rules.mapping: flattened into `cna_graphics_device_manager_subscribe_preparing_device_settings`, whose handler receives the candidate configuration as a **read-only** `CNA_GraphicsDeviceInformation`. In XNA this event is how an application overrides device settings; **in this runtime nobody can**, because the canonical event-handler collection delivers its argument as a `const` reference and the argument type's mutable accessor is therefore unreachable from any subscriber, C++ or C. This ABI reports what a subscriber can actually do rather than inventing a power the canonical event does not grant. C never constructs the argument object
rules.tests: `GraphicsDeviceManagerSmoke.c` subscribes to the event, applies changes and re-creates the device, and asserts that whatever the handler observed carried a real back-buffer width

rules.mapping: `cna_graphics_device_manager_create`, which takes the game handle the canonical constructor takes a pointer to. Creating the manager registers it as both the graphics device manager and the graphics device service, and a game accepts exactly one: a second creation reports the canonical refusal as `CNA_RESULT_INVALID_ARGUMENT`
rules.tests: `GraphicsDeviceManagerSmoke.c` creates one, asserts both services appear where none did before, and asserts the second creation is refused with its output left invalid

rules.mapping: `cna_game_get_content_manager_ext`, which answers a **borrowed** content-manager handle, and `cna_game_set_content_manager_ext`, which copies. A game owns its manager as a value member, so the borrow is the whole contract: one handle answered every time, refused by `cna_content_manager_destroy`, released with the game rather than by a caller, and accepted by every other content-manager route. The setter copies because the canonical setter copies — the caller keeps its own manager and later changes to it never reach the game
rules.tests: `RuntimeGameSmoke.c` borrows the manager twice and asserts the same handle comes back, reads and sets the game's own root directory through it, asserts destroying it is refused while it stays usable afterwards, copies a manager into the game and checks the borrowed handle still addresses the game's own object, and covers the null-output and invalid-handle refusals

rules.mapping: No C mapping, and the reason is not a design choice: **`CNA::Runtime` is declared and defined nowhere**. All five of its methods would fail to link if anything called them, nothing in the tree calls them, no translation unit includes `CNA/Misc.hpp`, and the compiled runtime archive contains no `CNA::Runtime::` symbol at all — the repository's own `audit/include/CNA/Misc.hpp.audit.md` reached the same conclusion independently. This ABI cannot bind a symbol that does not exist. `RuntimeOptions` is a sound four-flag value on its own, but its only purpose is to parameterize `Initialize`, so mapping it alone would hand a C consumer a structure that configures nothing. If the facade is ever implemented, these rows become real work rather than a record
rules.tests: the `CApi_UnimplementedRuntimeFacade` CTest check inspects the built runtime archive and fails if any `CNA::Runtime::` symbol ever appears, so this record cannot go stale in silence; subsystem availability that a caller actually needs is answered by `cna_graphics_ext_is_available`, `cna_devices_ext_is_available` and the audio/renderer capability queries instead
